**The Tuner**

The house was the kind that had once had money in it and now had only the shape of money—tall windows, a staircase built for descending in a certain way, radiators like iron accordions that had not been warm in some time. The woman who let him in was maybe seventy, wearing a cardigan with one button done wrong, and she did not apologize for the cold.

"It's through there," she said. "It hasn't been touched since my husband."

He'd learned not to ask *since my husband what*. People finished the sentence when they wanted to.

The piano was a Bechstein upright, black, with a candle sconce still screwed to the front panel, which told him it was old enough to have been played by gaslight. Someone had put a lace runner on top and, on the runner, a bowl of something that had been potpourri and was now mainly dust. He moved the bowl. She did not stop him.

"I'll need about two hours," he said. "Maybe more. It'll sound terrible for a while before it sounds right."

"I know how it works," she said. "He tuned it himself. Badly."

He opened the lid and the fallboard and pressed middle C. It gave him a sound like a bell dropped in a well—nearly the right pitch, then a wobble, then a fade that ended somewhere flat. He ran up the octave. Everything was low. The whole instrument had sagged, as instruments do when nobody asks anything of them. Eight or nine years, he guessed, from the drift. Maybe ten.

She sat down in a chair by the window with a book she did not open.

He took off the front panels and set them against the wall. The hammers were felted in a color that had been white when it was new and was now the color of an old man's undershirt. A little moth-work on the dampers, nothing fatal. Someone had written, in pencil on the inside of the frame, *tuned March 1988 — H.* and beneath it, in a different hand, a different pencil, *he means Feb.*

He set his mute strip, got out the lever, and started with the temperament octave, as he always did, because if you don't get the middle right there is no point getting anything else right.

There is a thing that happens in tuning that he had never been able to explain to anyone who didn't do it. You strike two strings that are supposed to be the same note, and if they are not the same, you hear a beating—a slow pulse, *wah, wah, wah*, the two frequencies disagreeing at the rate of their disagreement. You turn the pin a hair. The beating quickens, then slows, then slows more, then—and it is always sudden, the way a plane's landing is sudden after all that descending—it stops. The two strings become one string. The sound goes still and round. It is the closest thing he knows to watching something forgive something.

He did that two hundred and thirty times, more or less, over the course of the afternoon.

Somewhere around the tenor octave she said, without looking up from the book she wasn't reading, "He played every night. Not well. The same six or seven things. There was a Schubert he never got through without stopping in the same place."

"Which place?"

"I couldn't tell you the bar. There's a bit where the left hand has to go somewhere and the right hand has to stay and he could never make them do both."

He nodded and went on. F, F-sharp, G. The room was getting darker, the tall windows going from grey to a deeper grey, and she did not turn on a lamp, and he did not ask her to. He could tune in the dark. Most of it was ears.

"I thought about selling it," she said later. He was into the high treble now, the little brittle notes that fight you, that will not hold a pitch because there is so little string to hold it with. "A man came and looked at it and gave me a number and I said I'd think about it. That was three years ago. I don't know what I was waiting for."

He thought she might be waiting for him to say something, so he said, "It's a good instrument. The number was probably low."

"It wasn't about the number."

"No," he agreed. "It usually isn't."

He finished the top, then went back down and checked his unisons, the way you go back through a house checking the windows. A few had slipped. They always do—the whole instrument is under tons of tension, and when you change one part of it the rest shifts, sulks, resettles. He touched them up. Then he put the panels back on, and moved the dusty bowl back onto the lace runner, and sat down on the bench, which was too low for him, and played a scale, and then a chord, and then, because he could not quite help it, the opening of a Schubert impromptu, the G-flat one, the one everyone knows even if they don't know they know it.

He got about twelve bars in, to a place where the left hand has to go somewhere and the right hand has to stay.

He stopped there. Not because he couldn't manage it. He could. He stopped because he heard, behind him, the small sound of a book being closed that had never been opened, and he understood that the sentence had just been finished, and that it did not require his help.

He stood and gathered his tools. The room was nearly dark now.

"It'll want doing again in six months," he said. "It'll drift after a change like that. After that, once a year is fine."

"Once a year," she said.

At the door she paid him in cash, counted out slowly, the way people count when they are thinking about something else. Then she said, "Thank you," and he said it was nothing, which was not true, but which is what one says.

Walking to the van he heard, faintly, through the tall cold windows, a single note struck and held until it disappeared. Then another. Then nothing for a long time, and then the beginning of something, badly, in the dark.
